sources.entry: transfer.sh - Easy file sharing from the command line. MIT Go

summary.one_liner: transfer.sh is a self-hostable Go server for easy command-line file sharing, letting users upload a file with curl and get back a download link.
summary.what_it_does: The repository contains the transfer.sh server, which you run on your own machine or host to accept uploads via simple HTTP PUT requests (for example with curl --upload-file). Files are stored through a configurable provider: Amazon S3, Google Drive, Storj, or the local file system. The server supports optional features such as per-upload download limits (Max-Downloads), expiry in days (Max-Days), server-side AES256 encryption with a password, a delete URL returned in the X-Url-Delete response header, VirusTotal submission, and ClamAV prescanning. Access can be restricted with IP whitelists/blacklists, HTTP basic auth, and rate limiting, and TLS is supported via Let's Encrypt or your own certificates. The README also includes bash/zsh shell functions for uploading files and zipping directories.
use_cases: share a file from the command line with curl
run a private file-sharing server for your team
upload files to S3 or Google Drive via a simple HTTP endpoint
send temporary download links that expire or have a download limit
encrypt files before or during upload with gpg or server-side AES256
self-host a transfer.sh-style service with TLS and auth
notable: Pluggable storage backends: local disk, Amazon S3 (including custom S3-compatible endpoints), Google Drive, and Storj
Per-upload options via HTTP headers: Max-Downloads, Max-Days, and server-side AES256 encryption
Official Docker images including a recommended non-root variant (-noroot tags)
Optional ClamAV prescan and VirusTotal submission of uploads
caveats: The README opens with a security warning: IP filter and HTTP auth can be bypassed via unauthenticated X-Forwarded-For header spoofing.
The README advises against using the 'latest' Docker tag with auto-update tools because it may reference unreleased builds.
Server-side encryption is flagged as something to use only on a self-hosted server; the README discourages trusting third-party services with it.
